articles.title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional
articles.summary: After a decade-long legal battle, the Privy Council has overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep Trinidad and Tobago’s colonial-era “buggery law” on the books.
articles.content:
Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.

It has been a long road to get to this point. Almost as soon as the 2018 judgement went in Jones’ favour, the Trinidad and Tobago government announced its intention to appeal, with then Attorney General Faris Al-Rawi stating, “The rights of equality in the Constitution are clearly expressed. A first-instance decision is not the only decision to rely upon to settle the law. [An appeal] is only prudent so we can conclusively put the matter to rest.”

Almost seven years later, on March 25, 2025, a local appeal court overturned the 2018 judgement. Jones was disappointed but not deterred, vowing to take the case all the way to the Privy Council. He remained true to his word and on November 10, 2026 — quite ironically, given that it was a colonial-era law — British lawlords finally ruled on the matter.

There were a few key issues to be considered, including how to address the controversial “savings law” clause in the legislation — laws enacted prior to colonised countries becoming independent and developing their own constitutions, that were “saved” to remain in force even afterwards. Jones maintained that the clause had “no place in a 21st century democracy” and that Trinidad and Tobago’s government and parliament were “derelict” in not removing it, especially after the twin-island nation became a republic in 1976.

The Council’s conclusion in the case, which deemed that “Sections 13 and 16 of the SOA 1986 have been shown by Mr Jones ‘not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual,’” caused it to agree with the 2018 ruling and deny the attorney-general’s cross-appeal.

With other regional territories also using the Privy Council as their highest court of appeal, the result could augur well for similar actions across the wider Caribbean. As Jones told reporters on the steps of Trinidad’s Hall of Justice following his 2018 triumph, “The human rights issue is not just local […] Over 75 million Commonwealth citizens are criminalised using similar laws — 37 Commonwealth nations — criminalised similarly to Trinidad.”

Still, Jones — who launched his legal challenge in 2015 — says that the fight continues: “Whilst I welcome this judgement, it does not, however, address the main issues of human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial-era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond.” It is a stance echoed by many LGBTQ+ organisations, as issues of discrimination, language, and societal and religious acceptance also persist. Jones is well aware that changing these attitudes requires broader reform and re-education.

The law lords’ unanimous, provisional view, however, was that the original High Court remedy should stand. However, there may well be written submissions still to come.

Reactions from both within and beyond the LGBTQ+ community soon followed. Facebook user Ian Ragoonanan described the Privy Council ruling as “the law finally [catching] up with basic human dignity,” while academic Richard Drayton felt that the most important paragraph in the Privy Council judgement read: “[T]he rights in Sections 4 and 5 of the Constitution develop over time, since the Constitution is a living instrument capable of reflecting contemporaneous understandings of constitutional values […] The longer the passage of time, the more likely it is that those values will have developed in modern society and the more likely it is that the Constitution has to be interpreted accordingly.”

Pride TT, meanwhile, celebrated the victory: “We salute Jason Jones for his courage, resilience and unwavering determination, and recognise the advocates, allies and organisations who have stood alongside this fight for justice.” More than a mere legal milestone, it said, the judgement was “a reminder that everyone deserves to live with dignity, privacy and freedom from discrimination.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports a landmark legal victory overturning colonial-era laws criminalizing consensual same-sex acts in Trinidad and Tobago, affirming constitutional human rights and dignity. The decision has broad significance for LGBTQ+ rights across multiple Commonwealth countries sharing similar laws, representing a major step forward in human rights and equality. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a substantive legal and social breakthrough with meaningful impact beyond a single nation.
articles.personality_title: Trinidad and Tobago’s top court strikes down colonial law criminalizing same-sex acts
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Trinidad and Tobago had a law from colonial times that made anal sex between consenting adults illegal. This law was challenged by LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones, who argued it violated the country’s constitution.

**What happened** – After a long legal fight starting in 2015, the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which is still the highest court for Trinidad and Tobago, ruled in November 2026 that this law is unconstitutional. This decision reversed a 2025 local court ruling that had kept the law in place.

**Impact** – This ruling means the colonial-era “buggery law” can no longer be used to criminalize private, consensual acts between adults in Trinidad and Tobago. It also challenges a similar law clause that many former colonies still have, opening the door for other countries in the Caribbean and Commonwealth to follow this example. It affirms the rights and freedoms of LGBTQ+ individuals in a clear legal way.

**What's next step** – The fight for full equality and acceptance continues, as this ruling only removes one legal barrier. Jason Jones and LGBTQ+ groups say more work is needed to change social attitudes and laws that still discriminate. Other countries with similar laws may bring their own cases to the Privy Council or other courts inspired by this decision.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Privy Council’s ruling ends the use of a colonial law to criminalize same-sex acts in Trinidad and Tobago, marking an important legal victory for LGBTQ+ rights in the Caribbean and beyond.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Cour suprême de Trinité-et-Tobago annule une loi coloniale criminalisant les relations homosexuelles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Trinité-et-Tobago avait une loi datant de l’époque coloniale qui rendait illégale la sodomie entre adultes consentants. Cette loi a été contestée par l’activiste LGBTQ+ Jason Jones, qui soutenait qu’elle violait la constitution du pays.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Après une longue bataille juridique commencée en 2015, le Comité judiciaire du Conseil privé du Royaume-Uni, toujours la plus haute juridiction pour Trinité-et-Tobago, a statué en novembre 2026 que cette loi est inconstitutionnelle. Cette décision a annulé un jugement local de 2025 qui maintenait la loi.

**Impact** – Cette décision signifie que la « loi sur la sodomie » d’époque coloniale ne peut plus être utilisée pour criminaliser les actes privés et consentants entre adultes à Trinité-et-Tobago. Elle remet aussi en question une clause similaire que beaucoup d’anciennes colonies possèdent encore, ouvrant la voie à d’autres pays des Caraïbes et du Commonwealth pour suivre cet exemple. Elle affirme clairement les droits et libertés des personnes LGBTQ+.

**Prochaine étape** – La lutte pour l’égalité et l’acceptation complète continue, car ce jugement ne supprime qu’un obstacle légal. Jason Jones et les groupes LGBTQ+ disent qu’il faut encore changer les attitudes sociales et les lois discriminatoires. D’autres pays avec des lois similaires pourraient déposer leurs propres recours, inspirés par cette décision.

**Une phrase clé** – Le Conseil privé met fin à l’utilisation d’une loi coloniale criminalisant les actes homosexuels à Trinité-et-Tobago, marquant une victoire juridique importante pour les droits LGBTQ+ dans les Caraïbes et au-delà.
articles.personality_title_es: La corte superior de Trinidad y Tobago anula ley colonial que criminalizaba actos homosexuales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Trinidad y Tobago tenía una ley de la época colonial que prohibía el sexo anal entre adultos que daban su consentimiento. Esta ley fue impugnada por el activista LGBTQ+ Jason Jones, quien argumentó que violaba la constitución del país.

**Qué pasó** – Tras una larga batalla legal iniciada en 2015, el Comité Judicial del Consejo Privado del Reino Unido, que sigue siendo la corte más alta para Trinidad y Tobago, dictaminó en noviembre de 2026 que esta ley es inconstitucional. Esta decisión revocó un fallo local de 2025 que mantenía la ley vigente.

**Impacto** – Este fallo significa que la ley colonial que criminalizaba actos consensuados entre adultos ya no puede usarse en Trinidad y Tobago. También cuestiona una cláusula similar que muchas excolonias aún tienen, abriendo la posibilidad para que otros países del Caribe y de la Mancomunidad sigan este ejemplo. Afirma claramente los derechos y libertades de las personas LGBTQ+.

**Próximo paso** – La lucha por la igualdad y la aceptación continúa, ya que este fallo solo elimina un obstáculo legal. Jason Jones y grupos LGBTQ+ dicen que aún es necesario cambiar las actitudes sociales y leyes discriminatorias. Otros países con leyes similares podrían presentar sus propios casos inspirados en esta decisión.

**Resumen en una frase** – La decisión del Consejo Privado termina con la ley colonial que criminalizaba actos homosexuales en Trinidad y Tobago, marcando una victoria legal importante para los derechos LGBTQ+ en el Caribe y más allá.
